title: How to create a rule in Apple Mail on Mac: sort incoming email, step by step
metaTitle: How to Create a Rule in Apple Mail on Mac (Step by Step)
description: Learn how to create a rule in Apple Mail on Mac. Open Mail > Settings > Rules, set conditions, pick a mailbox, and sort new mail automatically.
targetKeyword: how to create a rule in apple mail on mac
secondaryKeywords: create a mail rule in Apple Mail
intro: To create a rule in Apple Mail on Mac, choose Mail > Settings, click Rules, then click Add Rule. Name the rule, set a condition such as a sender or subject, choose Move Message to a mailbox, click OK, and decide whether it covers mail you already have.
tldr: Open Mail > Settings, click Rules, then click Add Rule.
Give the rule a description, set one or more conditions, and choose an action such as Move Message to a mailbox.
Click OK, then choose whether the rule applies to existing messages or only to new ones.
Rules run from top to bottom. Drag them to change the order, and clear a checkbox to pause a rule.
If a rule stops working, reselect its mailbox, check for an earlier Stop Evaluating Rules action, or run it with Message > Apply Rules.

blocks.text: Apple Mail rules are the built-in way to sort incoming mail on a Mac. A rule checks each new message against conditions you set, then acts on the messages that match. The action most people use is Move Message to a mailbox. This page covers that path, plus the checks that keep a rule from catching the wrong mail.

Apple's Mail guide covers macOS 27 Golden Gate and also macOS Tahoe 26. The labels in the rule window can shift slightly between versions. Apple's full dialog text was only partly available when this page was written, so if a label on your screen differs, look for the control that does the same job.
Choose conditions that match the mail you want to sort

A condition tells Mail what to look for. Each row has a pop-up for the part of the message to check, such as From or Subject. A second pop-up sets the test, such as Contains, and a text box holds the words to match.

Picking the right field matters more than picking clever words. A sender's address rarely changes, so From is steady for bills and newsletters. Subject changes with every message, so a subject rule needs words that stay the same, such as receipt or invoice.

items: From: best for bills, banks, and newsletters that always send from one address.
Subject: best for fixed words such as receipt, invoice, or order confirmation.
To or CC: best for mail sent to a shared address or to a project group you belong to.
Several conditions together: use all when one condition alone catches too much.

blocks.text: Here is a worked case. You want receipts from your bank in a Finances mailbox. Set the rule to all, add From with your bank's address, and add Subject with the word receipt. Requiring both cuts false matches, since a marketing email from the same bank probably does not say receipt in its subject.
Test your words on a few real messages before you trust a rule. Open a message from the sender and read its subject line. Match the exact wording you see, not the wording you hope for.
Decide whether a rule covers mail you already have

When you click OK on a new rule, Mail asks whether to apply it to existing messages or only to new ones. Choose existing messages if you want an old pile of receipts sorted now. Choose new messages only if the old mail can stay where it is.

A rule for new messages works over time, so you do nothing once it is saved. A rule for existing messages works once, on mail that is already filed. A bulk move makes a bad match harder to spot, so check the results before you walk away.

blocks.title: Test before you apply to existing mail
blocks.text: Run a new rule on a narrow condition first. Then widen it once the results look right. A broad rule applied to old mail can move a large batch in one go.
Order matters when several rules apply

Mail runs rules from top to bottom in the Rules list. A message that matches an earlier rule can be handled before a later rule sees it. Drag rules up or down to set the order, and put narrow rules above broad catch-all rules.

A rule with a Stop Evaluating Rules action tells Mail to stop checking later rules for that message. Use that action on purpose, and check for it when a rule seems to skip mail. To pause a rule without deleting it, clear its checkbox. Only rules with a selected box run.

Duplicate copies a rule so you can edit the copy. That beats building a near copy from scratch, and it keeps the conditions you already tested. Remove is for rules you no longer need, so use it after you are sure.
Run rules by hand with Apply Rules and its shortcut

Mail normally runs rules as messages arrive. To run active rules on mail already in your mailboxes, choose Message > Apply Rules. This is the quickest way to test a new rule, and it is the fallback when a rule seems to ignore mail.

The shortcut for this is less settled than it should be. Apple's keyboard shortcuts page lists Apply active Mail rules as ⌃⌘L. A macOS Tahoe 26.0.1 thread on Apple Community gives Option + Command + L, ⌥⌘L, for the same job. Open the Message menu on your Mac and read the shortcut shown there. That is the one that counts on your machine.
Rules compared with Smart Mailboxes and Mail's own sorting

A rule moves messages into a mailbox. A Smart Mailbox only collects them. To make one, choose Mailbox > New Smart Mailbox, enter a name, pick a condition type in the first pop-up, add conditions, choose any or all when you have two or more, then click OK.

Use a Smart Mailbox when you want to look at a group of messages without changing where they are filed. Use a rule when you want the mail to end up in one particular place. Many people use both, with a rule filing receipts and a Smart Mailbox showing them in one list.

Mail also sorts some incoming messages into Primary, Transactions, Updates, and Promotions on its own. That sorting is separate from your rules. If a message lands somewhere you did not expect, check that category before you blame your rule.
Rules on other Macs and on iCloud.com

Rules you make on a Mac sync to your other Macs when iCloud Drive is on and Mail is selected in iCloud Drive options. Files attached to a rule, such as a sound file or a script, do not sync. Recreate those by hand on each Mac.

Mail on the web works differently. Go to icloud.com/mail, click the settings button above Mailboxes, choose Settings, select Rules, and click Add in the top-right corner. iCloud Mail on the web allows up to 500 rules. A new or changed rule can take up to 15 minutes to affect incoming email, so wait before you judge it.
Mistakes people make with rules

items: Using one broad condition, such as Subject contains order, that catches unrelated mail. Add a second condition to narrow it.
Leaving the any or all choice on the wrong setting, so the rule matches far more or far less than you meant.
Assuming the bottom rule wins. Mail runs rules from top to bottom, so an earlier match can take the message first.
Applying a new rule to existing messages before testing it, which moves a batch you did not mean to move.
Forgetting to select the rule's checkbox, then wondering why nothing happens.

blocks.text: Sorting is not only about tidiness. Microsoft Research followed 40 information workers across two workweeks. The study linked more time spent on email with lower perceived productivity and higher stress. A study like this does not prove a rule will fix your day, but fewer interruptions from mail is a fair goal.
Worked examples you can copy

A few rules cover most needs. Write each one down before you build it, so you know the condition, the mailbox, and whether it should cover old mail. The examples below use the same steps you saw earlier.

items: Receipts: all conditions. From contains your bank's address. Subject contains receipt. Action: Move Message to a mailbox called Finances.
Newsletters: one condition. From contains the newsletter's sender address. Action: Move Message to a mailbox called Newsletters. Apply to new messages only.
Project mail: any condition. To contains the project's shared address. CC contains the same address. Action: Move Message to the project mailbox. Test on existing messages first.
Utility bills: all conditions. From contains the utility's domain. Subject contains bill. Action: Move Message to a mailbox called Bills.

blocks.text: Give each rule a description you will recognize later, such as Receipts to Finances. The description is what you see in the list. It is also the first thing you will check when a rule misbehaves.
Fixes when an Apple Mail rule is not working

When a rule seems idle, start with the basics. Confirm its checkbox is selected, its destination mailbox still exists, and no earlier rule stops evaluation. Then run it by hand with Message > Apply Rules. If it moves mail that way, the problem is timing or order, not the conditions.

Some people report that rules only run after they click Apply Rules. Others say rules vanish after a system update. Those reports appear in Apple Community threads about macOS High Sierra, Ventura, and Sonoma. An Apple Community specialist pointed people back to the rules guide and to list order. No confirmed fix was posted.
Keep rules working after macOS updates

After any update, open Mail > Settings > Rules. Check that each rule you need is still there and still checked. Keep a short written list of your rules and their mailboxes, so a missing rule takes minutes to rebuild instead of a guessing game.
Rules on iCloud.com can lag too. A new or changed rule can take up to 15 minutes to affect incoming email. Wait that long, then send a test message before you change the rule again.
Where to go next

Once your rules sort mail, the next problem is usually the sender that still gets through. A rule files mail, but it does not stop it, so [block a sender in Apple Mail on Mac](/how-to/block-a-sender-in-apple-mail) when a rule is not enough. If you send a lot of mail from Gmail, check how that account is set up in [Apple Mail on Mac](/how-to/use-gmail-in-apple-mail-in-gmail). Schedule outgoing messages with [send later](/how-to/schedule-an-email-to-send-later-in-apple-mail).

faq.question: Does Apple Mail on Mac sort mail on its own once I make a rule?
faq.answer: Yes. A saved rule with its checkbox selected runs on new messages as they arrive. Rules run in list order, from top to bottom. If a rule seems to skip mail, reselect its destination mailbox and check for an earlier Stop Evaluating Rules action.

faq.question: Where do I find rules in Apple Mail on Mac?
faq.answer: Choose Mail > Settings, then click Rules. The Rules pane has Add Rule, Edit, Duplicate, and Remove buttons, and a checkbox beside each rule.

faq.question: What is the difference between a rule and a Smart Mailbox?
faq.answer: A rule moves matching messages into a mailbox. A Smart Mailbox gathers matching messages into one list without moving them. Use a rule to file mail and a Smart Mailbox to find it again.

faq.question: Can rules apply to mail I already have?
faq.answer: Yes. When you click OK on a new rule, Mail asks whether to apply it to existing messages or only to new ones. You can also run active rules later with Message > Apply Rules.

faq.question: Do my rules sync to my other Macs?
faq.answer: They do when iCloud Drive is on and Mail is selected in iCloud Drive options. Files attached to a rule, such as a sound file or a script, do not sync, so recreate those on each Mac.

faq.question: Which keyboard shortcut runs rules by hand?
faq.answer: Apple's keyboard shortcuts page lists Apply active Mail rules as ⌃⌘L. A macOS Tahoe 26.0.1 thread on Apple Community gives ⌥⌘L. Check the Message menu on your Mac to see which one it shows.

faq.question: How many rules can I make on iCloud.com?
faq.answer: Mail on iCloud.com allows up to 500 rules. A new or changed rule can take up to 15 minutes to affect incoming email, so wait before you judge it.

faq.question: Why does my Gmail rule seem to only add a label?
faq.answer: A community thread suggests that on some Gmail IMAP setups, the Move Message action may only apply a label. Test with one message first, then check how the account is set up in Mail.

steps.name: Open Mail settings
steps.text: Open Apple Mail and choose Mail > Settings from the menu bar. The Settings window opens with tabs across the top, and Rules is one of them.
steps.tip: Mail is the app menu next to the Apple menu. Make sure Mail is the active app before you open it.

steps.name: Open the Rules pane
steps.text: Click Rules in the Settings window. The Rules pane lists your existing rules in order, each with a checkbox beside it.
steps.tip: Rules run in list order from top to bottom, so the order you see here matters.

steps.name: Click Add Rule
steps.text: Click Add Rule. Mail opens a new rule form. Edit, Duplicate, and Remove sit with it for later changes.

steps.name: Enter a description
steps.text: Type a Description for the rule. This is the name you see in the list, so pick something you will recognize later, such as Receipts to Finances.

steps.name: Choose any or all
steps.text: Open the pop-up in the sentence that reads If any or all of the following conditions are met. Choose all when every condition must match. Choose any when one match is enough.

steps.name: Set the first condition
steps.text: Open the first pop-up and pick the part of the message to check, such as Subject or From. Open the second pop-up to pick the test, such as Contains. Type the words in the text box beside it.

steps.name: Add or remove conditions
steps.text: Click Add at the end of a row to add another condition. Click Remove to delete one. Set every pop-up in each new row before you move on.
steps.tip: Add two conditions when one alone catches too much mail.

steps.name: Choose the action
steps.text: Under Perform the following actions, open the pop-up and choose Move Message to a mailbox. Then pick the mailbox where matching mail should go.

steps.name: Click OK
steps.text: Click OK to save the rule. Mail then asks whether to apply it to existing messages or only to new messages. Pick the option that matches the mail you have.

steps.name: Confirm the checkbox
steps.text: Check that the rule's checkbox is selected in the Rules list. A rule runs only when its box is selected. Drag the rule up or down to change its place in the order.
steps.tip: A rule with a cleared checkbox looks saved but never runs.

steps.name: Test it with Apply Rules
steps.text: Open the Message menu and choose Apply Rules to run active rules on mail you already have. Then open the destination mailbox and check what moved.
steps.tip: Apple's shortcut table lists ⌃⌘L. A community post gives ⌥⌘L. Check the Message menu on your Mac.

shortcuts.action: Apply active Mail rules (Apple's listed shortcut)
Apply Rules, as a community thread gives it on macOS Tahoe 26.0.1

troubleshooting.problem: Rule does not run when new mail arrives
troubleshooting.fix: Reselect the destination mailbox in the rule and click OK. Check for an earlier rule with a Stop Evaluating Rules action, since it can block later rules. Then run the rule by hand with Message > Apply Rules to confirm it works.

troubleshooting.problem: Rule only runs when I click Apply Rules
troubleshooting.fix: Some Apple Community users report this on several macOS versions. Confirm the checkbox is selected and the rule sits above any rule that stops evaluation. An Apple Community specialist pointed to list order and Message > Apply Rules, and no confirmed fix has been posted.

troubleshooting.problem: Rules disappeared after a macOS update
troubleshooting.fix: Users report this on several macOS versions, but no confirmed fix exists. Open Mail > Settings > Rules and check what is still there. Rebuild anything missing using the steps above, then keep a written list of your rules.

troubleshooting.problem: Shortcut for Apply Rules does not work
troubleshooting.fix: Apple's table lists ⌃⌘L while a community post gives ⌥⌘L. Open the Message menu and use the shortcut shown beside Apply Rules on your Mac.

troubleshooting.problem: Gmail rule adds a label instead of moving mail
troubleshooting.fix: On some Gmail IMAP setups, Move Message may only apply a label. Test one message first, then check how the account is set up in Mail.
Rules on iCloud.com can take up to 15 minutes to affect incoming mail. Wait a while, then send a test message before you change the rule again.
